title: B.C.'s newest crime fighter has a nose for finding hidden electronic devices
summary: Nyx, a rookie in the Surrey Police Service's cybercrime unit, is a two-year-old female Labrador retriever specially trained in sniffing out electronic device

image.caption: Surrey Police dog Nyx was trained by a U.S. company in electronic device detection. (Surrey Police Service)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Nyx, a rookie in the Surrey Police Service's cybercrime unit, is a two-year-old female Labrador retriever specially trained in sniffing out electronic device
2-year-old Labrador retriever named Nyx is trained to detect a compound common in electronic devices
The Lower Mainland's newest crime fighter has a nose for the job, not to mention floppy ears and a wagging tail.

Nyx, a rookie in the Surrey Police Service's cybercrime unit, is a two-year-old female Labrador retriever specially trained in sniffing out electronic devices — microSD memory cards, cameras, laptops, AirTags, thumb drives and the like — regardless of how small or how well-hidden they are.
How does she do it?

It starts with a sense of smell that is estimated to be tens of thousands of times more sensitive than a human's. Add to that four months of training to detect triphenylphosphine oxide, or TPPO, a compound common in electronic devices.
"It's located in every USB portal, every laptop — every electronic device has TPPO," said Nyx's handler, Sgt. Emily Ovington with the SPS.
Nyx and handler Sgt. Emily Ovington of the Surrey Police Service. (Surrey Police Service)
Ovington and Nyx were paired up by Jordan Detection K9 in Indianapolis last month.

Jordan Detection K9 founder Todd Jordan estimates his team has trained 330 electronic storage detection dogs since 2015. The vast majority of the dogs go to law enforcement agencies where they are making the biggest difference in child sexual exploitation investigations by locating hidden devices containing illegal material.

Jordan's first device detection dog, Bear, helped find devices that led to the high-profile conviction of Subway spokesman Jared Fogle, currently serving a 15-year prison sentence for child pornography — now described in Canadian law as child sexual abuse and exploitation material — and child sex tourism.

blocks.text: Bear was also instrumental in the case against former USA gymnastics coach Marvin Sharp, who was arrested for child pornography and molestation. Chewy, another of Jordan’s dogs, assisted in the sex trafficking investigation into Sean (Diddy) Combs.
Jordan says he receives almost daily news about the successes of his K9 graduates.

"The dogs are brought in on the search warrants and the handlers always call me to let me know what they’re finding," he said. "They're saying 96 to 97 per cent of the time the dogs are locating devices that have been missed by a human. That’s huge."
Incredible noses
Jordan says the best detection dogs have astounding skills.

"Even if [a perpetrator] uses creative ways of hiding devices, the dogs will still find them. They're finding them 18 feet (5.5 metres) in the air, hidden in ceilings and in attics. The dogs are able to find devices underwater," he said.
"Those are things that I can't take credit for. That's just how incredible the dogs’ noses are."
Nyx has only been on the job for a few weeks but has already conducted six successful searches, according to the SPS.

"These days, electronic evidence is one of the top priorities for us in pretty much every investigation," said Ovington. "So the ability for us to be able to find all that evidence is really, really crucial.

blocks.text: "Nyx can be deployed in so many different ways from homicide investigations to cybercrime investigations to domestic violence or child exploitation material as well. She can go in and find things that police would typically not be able to find at all, or find quickly."
The SPS says it's the first municipal force in B.C. with a device detection dog in its ranks.
Ovington says the handler-K9 partnership doesn’t end at when the workday is done. Besides being a specialized police asset, Nyx is also a member of her family.
"We go home together," smiled Ovington. "When we get home my husband and son are super excited to see her."
